lessons.title: Understand what makes your offer different
body:
Important principle
A product does not need to be completely unique to have a compelling Unique Value Proposition. The differentiation only has to be meaningful to the intended customer — not something nobody else has ever created. Most durable digital products are not the first of their kind; they're a version of something familiar that fits one specific customer's situation noticeably better than the alternatives they already know about.

What a Unique Value Proposition actually is
Your Unique Value Proposition (UVP) is a clear statement of the specific, meaningful reason your intended customer should choose your offer over the alternatives available to them — including doing nothing at all. It answers one question directly: why this, and not something else they could use instead?

Four words that get confused with each other
Your Product Description lists what the offer contains — the facts of what's inside, with no claim about why it matters relative to anything else. Your Positioning Statement (Module 7) explains who the offer is for, what problem it solves and what outcome it helps achieve — it frames the whole offer, but doesn't have to name what makes it different from a specific alternative. Your Tagline is a short, memorable marketing phrase — it can echo your UVP, but it's not a substitute for actually stating the difference. Your UVP is narrower than all three: it names the specific, meaningful difference and why that difference matters to this customer, relative to what else they could choose. Keep these distinct rather than treating them as four names for the same sentence — a later lesson keeps your UVP and your Module 7 positioning statement as two separate things, deliberately.

Three practical sources of differentiation
These are practical categories to help you look in the right places — not a validated scoring framework, and not mutually exclusive. Most real UVPs draw on more than one at once.
  • Outcome — your offer gets the customer to a result the alternatives don't reach as fully, as reliably, or as specifically for their situation.
  • Method — your offer gets to a similar result through an approach, structure or process that's genuinely easier, clearer or better suited to this customer than how the alternatives do it.
  • Experience — the alternatives may get the customer to a similar place, but your offer is faster to start with, requires less effort, needs less guesswork, or simply feels less frustrating to actually use.

What does NOT automatically make an offer unique
These six are common mistakes — things that feel like differentiation but, on their own, usually aren't:
  • More bonuses than competitors. Extra items aren't a meaningful difference if they don't address something the customer actually cares about — see Module 4's bonus-selection rules.
  • Using AI to build or deliver it. How a product was made is rarely what a customer is buying; most competitors can say the same thing, and it says nothing about the outcome.
  • A beautiful website or sales page. Design quality affects trust and conversion, but it isn't a reason the product itself serves the customer better.
  • A large number of lessons or pages. Volume isn't value — a shorter, clearer product that actually gets someone to the outcome usually beats a longer one that doesn't.
  • Words like “premium,” “ultimate” or “revolutionary.” These are claims, not differences — and Lesson 5.3 covers why making them without support actively damages trust.
  • Being cheaper. Price can be part of a positioning decision, but a lower price alone isn't a meaningful value proposition — it invites comparison on price alone, which usually isn't a fight a new, unproven offer wins.
None of these are disqualified from ever supporting a UVP — a genuinely well-designed bonus or a genuinely faster method still counts. The test is always the same: does this actually change the result or the experience for the customer, in a way they'd notice and care about — not just a feature you can point to.

Why this comes before naming and pricing
You already completed the research this module reuses: your target customer (Module 1), their main problem (Module 2), your offer stack and bonuses (Module 4). This module asks you to look at that same material through one new lens — not “what did I build,” but “why would this specific customer pick it over everything else they could do instead.” Module 6 (Pricing) and Module 7 (Naming & Positioning) both work better once that reason is written down clearly, which is why this module comes before them.
lessons.insight: Your offer does not need to be completely different. It needs to give the right customer a meaningful reason to choose it.

lessons.title: Find your competitive difference
body:
Revisit the alternatives from Module 1
When you mapped your target market in Module 1, you were already looking at what your customer does instead of buying from you. Bring that same list back here: direct competitors selling something similar, other digital products solving a related problem, courses covering the same ground, software or apps, freelancers or done-for-you services, free resources, doing it themselves (DIY), and doing nothing at all. A hypothetical social-media content planner's list might include other content-planning toolkits and courses, scheduling software like Buffer or Later, a freelance social media manager, free templates and YouTube tutorials, planning it manually in a notes app, and simply not planning ahead at all. Every one of these is a real competitor for the customer's time, money or attention — not only the products that look most like yours.

Where to research — the same venues as Module 1
You don't need new research methods here, just a sharper question to ask of the same sources: competitor websites and sales pages, digital product marketplaces (Gumroad, Etsy, Whop), Reddit and relevant subreddits, Threads and X, YouTube comments on related videos, written reviews of comparable products, software pricing and comparison pages, and freelancer or service-provider listings. Useful search patterns, with your own niche substituted in: “[product category] reviews,” “[competitor name] vs,” “best [product category] for [audience],” “[problem] alternatives,” and “[competitor name] complaints” — that last one in particular tends to surface exactly where an existing alternative is falling short.

Building a simple competitive comparison
For each alternative you find, it's worth noting: target audience, core problem addressed, format (course, template, software, service, freelancer, DIY), price, depth of guidance, support offered, speed to first result, ease of use, what's explicitly included, and what's missing or frequently complained about. You don't need all ten for every alternative — note whatever's actually available, and leave the rest blank rather than guessing. The brief for this module is explicit that this stays a simple comparison, not an elaborate dashboard: a short table or list per alternative is enough to support a real decision.

Features are not the same thing as meaningful differences
A feature is something your product has. A meaningful difference is something the customer actually experiences differently because of it.
FEATURE, NOT YET A DIFFERENCE
“Includes 20 editable templates.” A competing toolkit may also include templates — the count alone doesn't tell the customer why this one serves them better.
THE MEANINGFUL DIFFERENCE BEHIND IT
“A guided weekly planning process that turns a blank week into finished posts in one sitting” — versus a template pack that still leaves the customer to figure out what to actually say and when to post it. The difference isn't the templates; it's that the customer stops needing to plan the planning.
A second pair: “Includes a private community” is a feature. “The only option of the three we compared where someone will actually answer a stuck customer's specific question within a day” is the meaningful difference behind it, if that's actually true of your offer and not of the alternatives.

Looking for underserved needs
Alongside comparing features, look for gaps the alternatives leave unaddressed: a step customers consistently struggle with that no alternative actually solves, a format mismatch (everyone offers a course when this audience wants something quicker to apply), a support gap, a trust or credibility gap, a price-to-depth mismatch, or a complexity mismatch (alternatives assume more skill or time than this audience actually has). These are potential opportunities, not proof of unmet demand — treat a gap you notice in competitor reviews or comments as a hypothesis, and weigh it against your actual Module 1 and Module 2 research before building a UVP around it. A complaint you found once in a review is weaker evidence than a problem your own target customers raised repeatedly.

Working through the comparison
With your comparison in front of you, ask: which alternatives are genuinely closest to what I'm offering? Where do they fall short for the specific customer I mapped in Module 1? Which of those shortfalls does my actual offer stack from Module 4 already address — not could address, but does, right now? That last question matters: a difference your offer doesn't yet actually deliver isn't a UVP, it's a feature request for your own roadmap.
lessons.insight: Your strongest difference is not necessarily what your product has more of. It may be what your product makes easier, clearer or more useful.

lessons.title: Articulate your Unique Value Proposition
body:
Selecting the most meaningful difference
Review everything gathered so far — your target customer and alternatives from Module 1, the problem inventory from Module 2, your outcome statement from Module 3, your actual offer stack from Module 4, and the comparison you just built in Lesson 5.2. From that, select the single difference that's most meaningful to your specific customer, genuinely true of your actual offer today, and clearly distinct from your closest alternatives. Resist the urge to list three or four at once — a UVP that tries to say everything usually communicates nothing. If more than one candidate feels strong, pick the one that would matter most to a customer who is actually comparing you against their next-best alternative.

The UVP writing template
“For [target customer] who need [important outcome], [product or offer] provides [meaningful value or distinctive approach], helping them [practical benefit] without [important frustration or limitation, if supported].”
The final clause is conditional on purpose — only include “without [frustration or limitation]” if it's something your offer actually, verifiably avoids. A UVP that's four clauses long but only the first three are true is weaker than a shorter one that's entirely accurate.

Weak versus strong
WEAK
“The best content planning toolkit on the market.” — no named customer, no stated outcome, no actual difference, and a claim about “the market” nobody has verified.
STRONG
“For small business owners who need a week's worth of social content without starting from a blank page, the 7-Day Content Planner provides a complete planning system — not just templates — helping them turn ideas into finished posts in one sitting, without an ongoing scheduling subscription they don't need.” — names the customer, the outcome, the specific difference, the practical benefit, and a real, specific limitation it avoids.

A complete worked example — hypothetical
Continuing the hypothetical small business owner used throughout this app: the offer is The 7-Day Content Planner, for small business owners who post on social media but have no system for deciding what to post, whose main problem is running out of ideas and starting from a blank page every week, and whose desired outcome is planning a week's worth of posts without that blank-page struggle. The core deliverable is a step-by-step content-planning process with a content pillar framework and a weekly planning workflow, plus bonuses addressing design, captions and a calendar. The alternatives considered in Lesson 5.2 included a template-only marketplace listing, a scheduling-software subscription, a freelance social media manager, free tutorials, and doing it manually. The possible differentiation identified: unlike the template-only listing, this offer includes the actual planning process, not just design files; unlike the scheduling subscription, it's a one-time purchase that teaches a repeatable method instead of charging monthly for a tool. The resulting UVP: “For small business owners who need a week's worth of social content without starting from a blank page, the 7-Day Content Planner provides a complete planning system — not just templates — helping them turn ideas into finished posts in one sitting, without an ongoing scheduling subscription they don't need.” This is a hypothetical illustration built from this app's own running example, not a real product or a claim about any actual competitor.

Claims to avoid
A UVP loses credibility the moment it makes a claim you can't actually support. Avoid: “the only product of its kind” (almost never verifiable, and rarely true), “the best on the market” (a claim about every competitor, which you haven't actually reviewed), “guaranteed to outperform” (a guarantee about a competitive comparison you don't control), “the fastest method” (a specific, checkable claim — don't make it unless you've actually checked it), and “completely unique” (contradicts this module's own opening principle — meaningful is the bar, not unprecedented). Every one of these invites a skeptical customer to ask “compared to what, exactly?” — a question your actual UVP should already be able to answer.

Keeping this distinct from your positioning statement
Module 7 will ask you to write a positioning statement using a who/format/outcome/obstacle structure for the whole offer. Your UVP feeds into that conversation but stays its own, separate statement — don't merge the two into one sentence. The positioning statement frames the offer; the UVP explains, specifically, why this one and not the alternative sitting next to it.
lessons.insight: Your UVP should communicate a difference your customer cares about and a value your product can actually deliver.

exercise.instructions: Name your closest alternative, what it doesn't cover, and the one meaningful difference your offer actually delivers — then write your UVP.

prompt.title: Unique Value Proposition Builder
prompt.purpose: Use this to pressure-test a meaningful, honest Unique Value Proposition against your real alternatives.
prompt.template: You are a positioning strategist helping someone identify and articulate a Unique Value Proposition (UVP) for a digital offer. My target customer: {{m1.topMarket}}. My problem inventory: {{m2.summary}}. My desired outcome: {{m3.outcomeStatement}}. My core deliverable and bonuses: {{m4.summary}}. My main competitive alternative and its limitation, if I've entered them: {{m5.mainAlternative}} / {{m5.alternativeLimitation}}. If any of the inputs above is missing or too thin — especially the target customer, problem, outcome, core deliverable and bonuses, and at least one real competitive alternative — ask me for it before doing any analysis. Using only what I've actually told you: compare my offer against the alternative(s) I've named, identify genuinely meaningful differences rather than surface-level features, and explicitly distinguish any feature you notice from the benefit or difference it actually produces for this customer. Explain in plain terms why each difference you identify would matter to this specific customer, not customers in general. Then draft 2–3 UVP options using this exact structure: "For [target customer] who need [important outcome], [product or offer] provides [meaningful value or distinctive approach], helping them [practical benefit] without [important frustration or limitation, if supported]." Only include the final "without..." clause where it's something I've actually told you is true. For each option, briefly state the reasoning behind it. Flag any option, phrase or claim that sounds unsupported, exaggerated, or like "the only/best/fastest/guaranteed/completely unique" rather than something this specific offer can actually back up. Never invent competitor features, customer reviews, market statistics, product performance figures, or a capability my offer doesn't actually have — if you don't have real information about an alternative, say so and ask, rather than filling the gap with a plausible-sounding guess.
